summary: Describes a mechanism to support the multicast needs of Layer 3 protocols over ATM networks, and applies it to IP multicasting. It addresses how a connection-oriented network can deliver one-to-many traffic.

eli5.summary: ATM normally connects two phones at a time. This note shows how to make it work like a conference call so one speaker reaches many listeners.

questions: how does ip multicast work over atm
what is mars multicast address resolution
what is a multicast server in atm
subtitle: How IP multicast gets a membership registry and one-to-many circuits on a network that only connects endpoints one pair at a time.

tldr.problem: IP multicast assumes the link layer can send to an abstract group address, but ATM under UNI 3.0/3.1 only offers point to point and point to multipoint virtual circuits where the sender must already know every receiver.
tldr.mechanism: A Multicast Address Resolution Server (MARS) keeps a registry that maps each layer 3 group address to the ATM addresses of its members. Endpoints ask it for the member list and build point to multipoint VCs, either a mesh of VCs or via an ATM level multicast server, and the MARS tells them about later joins and leaves.
tldr.outcome: Layer 3 protocols, IPv4 in particular, can multicast across an ATM cluster. Each group can use a VC mesh or a multicast server, and endpoints cannot tell which.

today: RFC 2022 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the text itself leaves several matters, such as backup MARS coordination, for future documents.

sections.title: The Multicast Problem on ATM
sections.content:
Network layer models such as the one in RFC 1112 assume a sender can address packets to an abstract multicast group and the link layer will deliver them, as Ethernet does. In IPv4 the group addresses are the range 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255. On Ethernet an algorithmic mapping turns a group address into an Ethernet multicast address, so no address resolution is needed to send.

ATM signalling as published in UNI 3.0 and UNI 3.1 has no such abstraction. Unicast uses point to point, bidirectional virtual circuits (VCs). Multicast uses point to multipoint, unidirectional VCs, and the key limitation is that the sender must know each intended recipient in advance and set up a VC with itself as root and the recipients as leaf nodes. Only the root may add or remove leaves.

The RFC has two goals: a group address registration and membership distribution mechanism for UNI 3.0/3.1 networks, and specific endpoint behaviours for managing point to multipoint VCs to carry layer 3 multicast. Quality of service is left out; VCs are requested with Unspecified Bit Rate (UBR) service by default. The text mostly follows the IPv4 model of RFC 1112 but notes it applies to other layer 3 protocols too.
sections.eli5: On a normal school bus everyone just hears the driver. ATM is more like single phone calls, so to talk to a whole class you need a list of who to call.

sections.title: VC Meshes and Multicast Servers
sections.content:
The RFC describes two ways to deliver a multicast packet over ATM. In a VC mesh, each sender sets up its own point to multipoint VC to every group member. A host that both sends and receives ends up originating one VC and terminating one for every other active sender, which is where the criss-crossing name comes from.

With a multicast server (MCS), each source opens a VC to the MCS, which reassembles the incoming AAL_SDUs and forwards them on a single point to multipoint VC to the real destinations. A side effect is that a sender that is also a member receives copies of its own packets back.

The trade-offs are spelled out. A mesh has no single congestion point, and likely gives higher throughput and lower latency, but each member must terminate a VC per sender. An MCS needs only 2 VCs per member (one out, one in) and a membership change touches a single VC, while a change in a mesh causes signalling at every sender. The MARS lets an administrator pick either approach on a group by group basis.
sections.eli5: A mesh is everybody phoning everybody directly. A multicast server is one person who takes all the messages and reads them out to the whole group. Phoning directly is faster, but the reader needs far fewer phone lines.

sections.title: The MARS and Its Clusters
sections.content:
The Multicast Address Resolution Server (MARS) is described as an extended analog of the ATM ARP server from RFC 1577. Where the ARP server stores {IP, ATM} pairs, the MARS stores {layer 3 address, ATM.1, ATM.2, ... ATM.n} mappings, learned dynamically or configured. It does not take part in actual multicasting of data packets.

Each MARS manages a Cluster: the set of ATM interfaces that choose to use direct ATM connections to multicast to each other, in practice the endpoints that share one MARS. To conform, administrators MUST give each Logical IP Subnet (LIS) its own MARS, a one-to-one mapping between cluster and LIS. Traffic between clusters passes through an inter-cluster device, in the IP case a multicast router.

Two control VCs carry membership news. ClusterControlVC is a point to multipoint VC from the MARS to all registered cluster members. ServerControlVC reaches all registered multicast servers. Between a client and the MARS there is also a transient point to point VC for queries, closed after an idle period with a suggested minimum of 1 minute and a recommended default of 20 minutes. A client is configured with the ATM address of its MARS.
sections.eli5: The MARS is the club secretary. Members tell the secretary when they join, and the secretary keeps the list and sends out announcements to everyone in the club.

sections.title: MARS Control Messages
sections.content:
By default MARS control messages are LLC/SNAP encapsulated with the codepoints 0xAA-AA-03, 0x00-00-5E and 0x00-03, which differ from ATMARP so a MARS and an ARP server can share a VC. A message has four parts: a fixed header, mandatory fields that depend on the operation, variable length addresses, and optional supplementary TLVs. A null address is encoded with zero length and takes no space.

The fixed header holds mar$afn (address family, 0x000F), mar$pro (the layer 3 protocol, 56 bits, such as 0x800 for IPv4), a reserved field, a checksum, the extensions offset mar$extoff, the operation code mar$op and the type and length of the source ATM number and subaddress. The checksum is the standard IP checksum over the whole message and may be skipped by setting it to zero, because the AAL5 CRC already protects the message.

Supplementary parameters are TLV elements starting on a 32 bit boundary and terminated by a Null TLV. The top 2 bits of the type tell a receiver what to do with a type it does not recognise. A conforming implementation only has to recognise the Null TLV.
sections.eli5: Every message starts with a standard label saying what kind of message it is and who sent it, followed by the details, so the same envelope can be reused for many purposes.

sections.title: Sending to a Group
sections.content:
When a layer 3 packet is passed down for a group with no open outgoing VC, the endpoint sends a MARS_REQUEST (op 1) with the group address as target. The MARS answers with one or more MARS_MULTI messages (op 2) listing member ATM addresses, or a MARS_NAK (op 6) if there are none, in which case the packet is silently discarded. Each MARS_MULTI carries an end-of-reply flag x and a sequence number y, and the client discards the reply and asks again if it detects a jump in y or a lost final part. The suggested timer for the last part is 10 seconds. The RFC's example shows that with 20 byte ATM numbers and a 9180 byte MTU, one MARS_MULTI can hold at most 456 addresses.

The endpoint then issues L_MULTI_RQ for the first address and L_MULTI_ADD for each other one, sends the packet, and keeps the VC as the active path for that group. Failed adds are retried after a random delay of 5 to 10 seconds that doubles on each failure, and the data may start flowing before all leaves are added. A VC is released after an inactivity timer, with a minimum of 1 minute and a recommended 20 minutes.

Multicast data uses its own LLC/SNAP encapsulation so a sender can detect reflected packets from an MCS. Clients MUST transmit using Type #1, which carries the sender's 2 octet Cluster Member ID before the protocol type, and MUST accept Type #1 or Type #2. A receiver silently drops a Type #1 packet whose CMI matches its own.
sections.eli5: Before talking to a group you ask the secretary who is in it, then phone each of them. If you see your own name on the incoming message, you ignore it.

sections.title: Joining, Leaving and Multicast Servers
sections.content:
An endpoint first registers by sending a MARS_JOIN (op 4) with the register flag set. The MARS adds it as a leaf of ClusterControlVC and assigns a 16 bit Cluster Member ID (CMI). To join a group it sends a MARS_JOIN with a <min,max> address pair, and MARS_LEAVE (op 5) to leave. The MARS rebroadcasts these on ClusterControlVC so senders can add or drop leaves with L_MULTI_ADD and L_MULTI_DROP. The client resends a join or leave until it sees a copy come back, with a recommended 10 second interval and failure after 5 retransmissions.

A pair can span a block of addresses, which lets a multicast router join the whole Class D space 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255 or only part of it. Routers can also send MARS_GROUPLIST_REQUEST (op 10) and get a MARS_GROUPLIST_REPLY (op 11) listing groups with layer 3 members, which the RFC recommends as a way to avoid sending IGMP queries into the cluster.

A multicast server registers with MARS_MSERV (op 3) and announces a group with it. For a group served by an MCS the MARS gives ordinary clients the server's address instead of the member list, and sends MARS_MIGRATE (op 13) to move existing senders from a mesh to the server. Members are passed to the MCS with MARS_SJOIN (op 18) and MARS_SLEAVE (op 19) on ServerControlVC. Without an MCS synchronisation protocol, an administrator MUST NOT allow more than one logical MCS for a group.
sections.eli5: To get on the list you tell the secretary your name and wait until they read it back to you. If the group has a reader, the secretary tells everyone to phone the reader instead of each other.

sections.title: Staying in Sync and Recovering
sections.content:
Members must not miss membership changes, so the MARS keeps a 32 bit Cluster Sequence Number (CSN) that goes up by one for every transmission on ClusterControlVC and is carried in the mar$msn field. Each client keeps its own Host Sequence Number and compares: if the difference is not 0 or 1, it has missed something and must revalidate. Revalidation re-issues a MARS_REQUEST per group and then adds or drops only the leaves that differ, while data keeps flowing. The VC_revalidate flag for each group is set at a random time between 1 and 10 seconds after a jump is detected.

Clients can also use backups. A client may hold a table of alternative MARS addresses. On a failure it waits a random 1 to 10 seconds, then re-registers and rejoins its groups, and if that fails it waits at least 1 minute before trying the next address. The MARS sends MARS_REDIRECT_MAP (op 12) on ClusterControlVC at least every 2 minutes, with 1 minute recommended, carrying its list of backups. A hard redirect re-registers and rejoins groups. A soft redirect just opens a VC to the new MARS and registers. The RFC says how backup MARSs coordinate with each other is for future work.
sections.eli5: Every announcement has a number on it. If you hear number 5 and then number 7, you know you missed one, so you go and ask the secretary for the full list again.

sections.title: Security and Open Issues
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section is a single sentence: security issues are not addressed in this document. The only trust check the text describes is for a soft redirect, where a cluster member must check that the node at the other end of the VC carrying the MARS_REDIRECT_MAP is the MARS it trusts.

The RFC lists open issues. These include coordination between backup MARSs, coordination between multiple MCSs, detecting dead cluster members beyond relying on the member dropping off ClusterControlVC, and ATM Group Addresses and Leaf Initiated Join, which were not addressed.
sections.eli5: The rulebook says nothing about keeping out troublemakers. It only lists some jobs the club still has to figure out.
